newsitem.title: albania: Berisha appoints new premier as unrest spreads.
newsitem.headline: Berisha appoints new premier as unrest spreads.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha appointed a new prime minister from the opposition Socialist Party on Tuesday in a bid to halt an armed rebellion sweeping the south.
The appointment came after news that the violence had spread to northern Albania for the first time since the insurgency broke out last month.
Up to 300 people forced their way into the barracks in Bajram Curri, over 200 km (130 miles) northeast of Tirana, and seized hundreds of Kalashnikov assault rifles.
Raiders had tried to break into the barracks on Monday evening but withdrew after soldiers fired into the air, a local political leader said.

Xhevded Mehmeti of the ruling Democratic Party said the looters were not obviously pro- or anti-Berisha. "One of them said ,'In the face of a state that is non-existant, we have to protect ourselves'," he told Reuters.
Several Western embassies advised nationals with no urgent business in the country to leave.
Berisha appointed Bashkim Fino, an economist from the southern town of Gjirokaster, now in rebel hands, to replace Aleksander Meksi of the Democratic Party, who quit as prime minister last week.
Berisha was also negotiating with political party leaders on the formation of a new national unity government to rule until new elections by June.
The Italian Foreign Ministry said Berisha telephoned Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini to tell him he had chosen a new premier and a new government would be set up within 24 hours.

Albania asked Italy to be guarantor of an agreement between Berisha and political leaders last week involving an interim government, new elections and an amnesty for rebels to surrender their weapons.
But rebel leaders in the south appeared to reject the deal, saying they would not hand back their arms unless Berisha resigned.
"Weapons won't be turned in without guarantees. Our basic demand is for Berisha to resign," said Fuad Karali, chief of rebel police in the southern port of Sarande.

The rebels accuse the president of failing to intervene over shady pyramid savings schemes that collapsed in January along with the life savings of thousands of families, particularly in the more prosperous south.

The appointment of a member of the Socialist party to the premiership was seen as a concession to the opposition, although the Sociatists have little or no influence over the highly localised rebel groups in the south.
The rebels now control the southwest Albania, from the Adriatic ports of Vlore and Sarande to the inland towns of Delvine, Gjirokaster, Tepelene, Permet and Berat.
In Vlore a rebel delegation agreed to Berisha's deal with opposition parties for new elections, but rebels elsewhere rejected any compromise while the president remained in power.
Around 150,000 assault rifles have been looted from barracks in the past week, along with tanks, anti-aircraft guns, heavy cannon and even fighter jets.

"Every family in southern Albania has at least one assault rifle," said Limpi Mango, a rebel leader in Permet. "One town after the next is falling to the people. It would be crazy to surrender our weapons. It would be like accepting defeat while you're winning."

With so many weapons available, the situation in rebel-held towns was volatile. In Sarande, looters ransacked and set fire to a hotel, ignoring a warning from the rebel-led council that looters would be punished.
On the Greek border, masked gunmen shot dead an Albanian man after he refused to hand over his money, the semi-official Athens News Agency said.
In Kucove, rebels were taking stock after seizing a major military airbase and taking control of about one fifth of Albania's warplanes.
Angry pilots in front of 19 ageing Mig fighters were bitter over losing money in the savings schemes and declared they could not obey orders to resist the insurgents.
